cards.text: Job lost his children and his wealth (Job 1:13-19), and then his health (Job 2:7). He just sat through a long speech from his friend Eliphaz the Temanite (Job 2:11; 4:1-5:27). Now it's Job's turn to answer, and friend, he has a LOT to say.
Job starts with a wish: if only his grief and his calamity could be placed on the scales together. Baker, I've weighed a LOT of flour in my day, and I have NEVER seen a scale built for that.

cards.question: Job says his grief would outweigh the sand of the seas. He says no wonder his words have been ___.

cards.text: Then Job says arrows have pierced him, and his spirit drinks in their poison. Friend, this is not a man having a little rough Tuesday.

cards.question: Job says arrows have pierced him and poisoned his spirit. Whose arrows does he say they are?

cards.text: Next, Job asks: does a wild donkey bray over fresh grass, or an ox low over its fodder? Friend, a donkey with fresh grass has NOTHING to complain about.

Then he asks if tasteless food is eaten without salt, or if there's any flavor in the white of an egg. I forgot the sugar in ONE batch once, baker, and those cookies tasted like cardboard that gave up on its dreams.

cards.question: Tasteless food without salt, the white of an egg. Job says food like that is loathsome to him.

cards.text: Then Job wishes that his request would be granted and that God would fulfill his hope.

cards.question: Job hopes God will grant his request. What does he hope God will be willing to do?

answers.text: Crush him and cut him off
Give back all that he lost

cards.question: Even through unrelenting pain, Job says one thing still brings him comfort and joy. What is it?

cards.text: Then Job asks what strength he has that he should still hope, and what future he has that he should be patient. You know when your phone hits 1% and there's no charger anywhere in the building?

cards.question: Job says his strength is like stone and his flesh is made of bronze.
Now that success is driven from him, Job says he still has plenty of help left within him.

cards.text: Now Job turns from his own pain to his friends. He has something to say about what a man in despair should get from a friend.

cards.question: Job says a despairing man should have something from his friend, even if he forsakes the fear of the Almighty. What is it?

cards.text: Then Job paints a picture. He says his brothers are as faithless as wadis, seasonal streams that overflow, darkened because of the ice and the melting snow.

cards.question: Wadis overflow when the snow melts. What does Job say happens to them in the dry season?

cards.text: Picture it, baker. Caravans turn aside from their routes, go into the wasteland and perish.

cards.question: Job names two groups of travelers who look for water and hope to find it. Where are they from?

cards.text: Job says the caravans had hoped, and their arrival brings disappointment. Baker, it's the buddy who says, "Call me ANYTIME," and when you call, it's straight to voicemail.

cards.question: Job tells his friends that right now they are no help. When they see terror, they are afraid.

cards.text: Then Job asks his friends a question about what he's ever asked them for. Oh, friend, he is pulling out the RECEIPTS.

cards.question: Job says he once asked his friends for a bribe from their wealth to rescue him.

cards.text: So what does Job want from his friends? He says, “Teach me, and I will be silent.”

cards.question: Job asks his friends to teach him. What does he ask them to help him understand?

cards.text: Job says, “How painful are honest words!” Then he asks what their argument even proves, like everybody walking out of a forty-minute meeting asking, "Okay... but what did we DECIDE?"

cards.question: Job asks his friends if they intend to correct his words and treat something of his as wind. What is it?

cards.text: Job says they'd even cast lots for an orphan and barter away their friend. Then he says, “But now, please look at me. Would I lie to your face?”

cards.question: Job asks his friends to reconsider and not be unjust, for his ___ is at stake.
Job ends his plea to his friends by admitting there is iniquity on his tongue.

cards.text: Now Job zooms out to everybody, asking if man's days aren't like a hired hand's: a slave longing for shade, a hireling waiting for his wages. You know that person refreshing the bank app at 11:59 PM, whispering, "Come on, direct deposit, COME ON"?

cards.question: Job compares man to a hired hand waiting on wages. Then he says he has been allotted months of rest and nights of peace.

cards.text: When Job lies down, he thinks, “When will I get up?” Baker, it's the night before a big early flight, staring at the ceiling and checking the clock every twenty minutes.

cards.question: The night drags on for Job. What does he do until dawn?

cards.text: Job describes his body: his flesh is clothed with worms and encrusted with dirt, and his skin is cracked and festering. I think this one hurts, friend.

cards.question: Job says his days are swifter than a weaver's shuttle, and they come to an end without ___.
Job says his life is but a breath, but his eyes will see happiness again someday.

cards.text: Job says, “You will look for me, but I will be no more.” Like a cloud that vanishes, the one who goes down to Sheol does not come back up.

cards.question: Job says the one who goes down to Sheol never returns to his house. What does he say about that man's place?
After all that, Job decides to hold his tongue and keep the anguish of his spirit to himself.

cards.text: Then Job asks God a big question: is he the sea, or the monster of the deep?

cards.question: Job asks God if he is the sea or the monster of the deep. What does Job say God must do to him?

cards.text: Job says that when he thinks his bed will comfort him, God frightens him with dreams and terrifies him with visions. The ONE place you're supposed to finally get a break, baker.

cards.question: Job says those dreams and visions are so terrifying that he would prefer death over his life in this body.

cards.text: Job says, “I loathe my life! I would not live forever.” Friend, he isn't hiding one bit of how he feels.

Then Job asks God, “What is man that You should exalt him, that You should set Your heart upon him…” and why God attends to him every morning and tests him every moment. Baker, I've read that line a hundred times, and it still stops me in my tracks.

cards.question: Job wonders why God attends to man every morning and tests him every moment. What does Job ask God next?

answers.text: Whether God will ever look away
Whether God will send him rain

cards.question: Job asks God, “If I have sinned, what have I done to You, O watcher of mankind?” Then he asks why God has made him something, so that he is a burden to God. What?
Near the end, Job asks God why He does not pardon his transgression and take away his iniquity.

cards.text: Job ends by saying he'll soon lie down in the dust, and God will seek him, but he'll be no more. That's where we leave it for now, friend, because this conversation is far from over.
